The answer lies in how generative tools rearrange the flow of information reaching working memory. When an open-source text tool renders a script's structure visible, students no longer spend effort parsing formatting conventions or reconstructing narrative scaffolding by hand; that housekeeping is offloaded, and the presentation-driven demand that ordinarily clutters early learning thins out 37 . The same logic extends to redundancy. Conventional animation instruction often forces learners to process the same content through several channels at once-verbal explanation layered over manual sketching-whereas the generative pipeline lets each channel do distinct work, trimming the duplicated processing that inflates extraneous load 13 . Freed capacity does not simply vanish, though. The selective response of the facets asks for a different explanation. Fluency and flexibility trade largely on retrieval speed and category switching, capacities that improve with practice in either condition, so it is unsurprising that they rose in both groups without a group difference 28 . Originality and elaboration depend instead on deeper transformation-combining remote associates, refining a concept until it holds together-and these operations draw on precisely the schema-building resources that germane load names 30 . On this reading the intervention did not make students think more; it changed the quality of thinking that the freed capacity could sustain, which is why the advantage concentrated in the two facets most sensitive to deep processing. The correlations in Fig. 7 sharpen that account. Fluency and flexibility hang together closely, as they should if both index the breadth of an initial search through memory, and their joint insensitivity to condition suggests that the generative toolchain did not simply accelerate idea retrieval. Originality and elaboration form a separate and more moderate pairing, and their weak association with fluency matters for interpretation: had originality risen only because students produced more responses, its correlation with fluency should have been considerably higher than the 0.41 observed. The same two-part structure has emerged from factor analyses of the Torrance battery, where fluency-driven and transformation-driven components separate rather than collapse into a single dimension 31 . Set against the long-run decline in originality and elaboration documented for large samples, the present result reads as a modest counterpoint, since the facets hardest to move historically are the ones this intervention moved 46 . Ulger's finding that creative training can lift divergent-thinking scores without touching problem-solving is a useful caution in the other direction: facet-level gains need not generalise to the wider construct 29 . The inverted-U finding for intrinsic load carries a caution that the earlier sections could only foreshadow. Too little intrinsic challenge leaves creative reasoning underpowered, while too much saturates working memory and crowds out the generative operations creativity needs 34 . The practical lesson is that intrinsic load should be tuned rather than minimised. A teacher designing an AIGC-supported animation task ought to calibrate conceptual difficulty toward the middle of the range-demanding enough to engage, restrained enough to leave room for exploration-rather than assuming that easier is always better 12 . The second concerns the shape of the intrinsic-load effect. A curvilinear relation is hard to reconcile with the standard prescription to minimise load, and it suggests that the prescription was always domain-bound, holding for schema acquisition but not for tasks whose value lies in exploration. The third concerns creativity theory. Because the four facets responded differently to one instructional manipulation, treating divergent thinking as a single latent ability discards information that a facet-level model retains-an argument the creativity literature has long made on psychometric grounds 31 and that an intervention study can now make on experimental ones. AIM To map kinematic AI evidence across eight predefined domains and assessed its quality relative to CADe and surgical AI. METHODS MEDLINE/PubMed, EMBASE-OVID, Cochrane, and IEEE Xplore were searched following Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses checklist (CRD420261320279). Studies applying AI to kinematic data in gastrointestinal endoscopy were eligible. Risk of bias used Cochrane Risk of Bias 2, Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2, and PROBAST + AI; certainty of evidence used GRADE. RESULTS Fifty-eight studies were included. Evidence generation was asymmetric: (1) Randomized controlled trial ratio approximately 5:1 (> 40 vs 8); (2) Patient ratio approximately 4:1 (> 27000 vs approximately 6200); (3) Annual publication ratio approximately 12:1; and (4) ≥ 6 vs 0 regulatory approvals favoring diagnostic AI. Withdrawal speed monitoring and coverage/blind-spot mapping reached moderate GRADE certainty, but all 8 randomized controlled trials were from China and 6 of 8 used the ENDOANGEL platform. The remaining six domains have not reached moderate certainty: (1) Workflow recognition and skill assessment are approaching clinical readiness; and (2) Autonomous navigation, robotic control, simultaneous localization and mapping/three-dimensional reconstruction, and instrument tracking remain at the engineering stage. Comparison with surgical AI indicated that the gap reflects ecosystem-level factors – absence of open datasets, benchmarking challenges, and regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI – rather than technical immaturity. CONCLUSION Kinematic AI addresses exposure errors that CADe cannot correct and has shown additive benefit alongside CADe. Two domains are ready for geographically diverse validation; six remain at the engineering stage. Priorities are open datasets, benchmarking infrastructure, and dedicated regulatory pathways for motion-acting AI.

reading.interpretation: This study examined the association between generative AI dependence and medical students' clinical reasoning and tested whether critical thinking statistically accounted for part of this association. The results showed that generative AI dependence was negatively associated with critical thinking, whereas critical thinking was positively associated with clinical reasoning. After critical thinking was included, the direct association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning remained significant, suggesting that critical thinking accounted for only part of this association. AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking, but high AI literacy did not eliminate this negative association. Given that this study used an observational, three-wave time-lagged design and did not include baseline measures, the results can only reflect associations among variables rather than strict causal relationships; pre-existing individual differences, reverse or reciprocal associations, and unmeasured time-varying confounders cannot be ruled out. In addition, the outcome in this study was self-reported Clinical Reasoning as reflected by diagnostic thinking disposition, rather than objectively demonstrated clinical reasoning performance, diagnostic accuracy, or patient safety outcomes. In summary, this study suggests that medical education should focus on fostering calibrated AI use, critical thinking, and AI literacy, rather than simply restricting AI use; future intervention studies are still needed to verify whether such educational strategies can actually improve medical students' clinical reasoning.

The results showed that generative AI dependence was negatively associated with critical thinking, whereas critical thinking was positively associated with clinical reasoning. After critical thinking was included, the direct association between generative AI dependence and clinical reasoning remained significant, suggesting that critical thinking accounted for only part of this association. AI literacy statistically moderated the negative association between generative AI dependence and critical thinking, but high AI literacy did not eliminate this negative association. Future studies should combine self-reported data with case studies and standardized objective clinical examination (OSCE) scores and other performance indicators. Because different systems may involve different capabilities, interaction patterns, and levels of output reliability, the sample should not be assumed to be homogeneous with respect to AI exposure. Future studies should therefore explore the differences among AI tools and specific types of medical learning tasks, and should collect detailed information on the types of GenAI systems used, the purposes and task contexts of use, and the frequency of use for each system. Independent replication would provide a stronger test of measurement stability. The very high reliability coefficients for AI literacy and clinical reasoning, together with their relatively high mean inter-item correlations, also suggest that some item overlap may be present. Future studies should evaluate whether shorter forms can retain construct breadth while improving measurement efficiency.

A meta-analysis of the 28 studies and 70 effect sizes found that chatbot-assisted language learning has a moderate positive effect compared with non-chatbot conditions, and this effect is moderated by educational level, language proficiency, interface design and interactional capability [1] . Together, these studies indicate that the effectiveness of AI is related to task authenticity, high-quality feedback and deep learner involvement.

The conflict between generative linguistics and generative AI is not absolute; rather, at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program, the two are in harmony. items.abstract_text: Abstract Purpose The primary objective of the study was to determine how clinically accurate and useful ChatGPT-4o–generated outputs are when identical prompts are entered simultaneously in 3 independent ChatGPT sessions utilizing the same user-facing model. The secondary objective was to identify whether differences in outputs affect clinical outcomes (ie, impact variability). Methods Five clinical prompts focusing on diabetes management and counseling were developed. Each clinical prompt was simultaneously inputted into 3 separate devices using ChatGPT-4o to generate outputs. Through a modified Delphi technique, 5 clinical pharmacy faculty members with expertise in diabetes management independently rated each ChatGPT-generated output for accuracy (poor, borderline, or good) usefulness (not useful, somewhat useful, or very useful) and impact variability (low, moderate, or high). After initial assessment, responses were collated and anonymously shared among the pharmacy faculty raters. The faculty members were invited to revise their evaluations based on collective feedback, then convened in a virtual panel with moderators to discuss evaluations and work towards consensus. Results Consensus was achieved for all ChatGPT outputs. Accuracy ratings ranged from borderline to good. Two of the clinical prompts yielded outputs that received different accuracy ratings, which may have impacted variability. Usefulness ratings ranged from somewhat useful to very useful, with one clinical prompt yielding outputs that received different usefulness ratings. Conclusion While ChatGPT-4o outputs were generally accurate and useful, limitations and inconsistencies were noted. Users should be aware simultaneously generated outputs across multiple devices using ChatGPT can vary in their accuracy and usefulness in diabetes management.

While GenAI can aid in learning, overreliance can lessen students' independent thinking.

Multiple patterns of using GenAI for problem solving were illustrated in the article by Hou et al. (2025) , suggesting that this reliance is not necessarily a problem; therefore, one should not assume that any student's use of GenAI for problem-solving is problematic. Another crucial explanation to consider is AI literacy. If students grasp the functionality of GenAI, the limitations of GenAI, the evaluation of the outputs, and the responsible use of GenAI, they may be less likely to give up their thinking skills to GenAI. Evaluation and responsible use are recurring themes that have been consistently highlighted as core aspects of AI and GenAI literacy in recent literature (Lintner, 2024; Chen et al., 2025; Park, 2025) .So, the educational task is not just about minimizing the students' use of GenAI. Rather, universities need to introduce students to using GenAI, but not transfer ownership of the thinking process to the technology. The learning potential of generative AI is newly available for universities, but it is highly reliant on how students use it. The present study suggests that overreliance on GenAI might have a relationship with student problem-solving ability via the cognitive offloading pathway and that AI literacy could affect the strength of this relationship. This is the key innovation of the model, as it asks a much more complex question of whether students use GenAI or not. Instead, it investigates how reliance on GenAI could alter students' thinking processes and if there is a way for students to have a way to remain independent in problem-solving with the support of AI literacy. The study thus offers a specific educational psychology approach for studying GenAI dependence in university education, as well as cognitive offloading and problem-solving.

This shift challenges a largely unexamined assumption in advertising theory: that persuasion operates through cognitive elaboration within the individual consumer.
